items.text: We argue that current techniques restrict the power of the pre-trained representations, especially for the ﬁne-tuning approaches.
items.why: Claims current pre-trained language representation techniques restrict representation power.
items.plain: We argue that current methods limit the power of pre-trained language representations, especially for fine-tuning.

items.text: The major limitation is that standard language models are unidirectional, and this limits the choice of architectures that can be used during pre-training.
items.why: Identifies standard language model unidirectionality as the major limitation.
items.plain: The main limitation is that standard language models process text in only one direction, which restricts the pre-training architectures we can use.

items.text: Such restrictions are sub-optimal for sentence-level tasks, and could be very harmful when applying ﬁnetuning based approaches to token-level tasks such as question answering, where it is crucial to incorporate context from both directions.
items.why: Claims unidirectional pre-training is sub-optimal and harmful for token-level tasks.
items.plain: These directional limits are sub-optimal for sentence-level tasks and can severely hurt fine-tuning on token-level tasks like question answering, where context from both directions is crucial.

items.text: BERTBASE was chosen to have the same model size as OpenAI GPT for comparison purposes.
items.why: Explains BERTBASE was sized specifically to match OpenAI GPT for fair comparison.
items.plain: We selected the size of BERTBASE to match OpenAI GPT so we could compare them directly.

items.text: Task #1: Masked LM Intuitively, it is reasonable to believe that a deep bidirectional model is strictly more powerful than either a left-to-right model or the shallow concatenation of a left-toright and a right-to-left model.
items.why: States the core premise that deep bidirectional models are strictly more powerful.
items.plain: Intuitively, a deep bidirectional model should be strictly more powerful than a left-to-right model or a shallow combination of left-to-right and right-to-left models.

items.text: Although this allows us to obtain a bidirectional pre-trained model, a downside is that we are creating a mismatch between pre-training and ﬁne-tuning, since the [MASK] token does not appear during ﬁne-tuning.
items.why: Acknowledges a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning caused by MASK tokens.
items.plain: While this approach enables a bidirectional pre-trained model, it creates a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning because the [MASK] token never appears during fine-tuning.

items.text: As we show in Figure 1, C is used for next sentence prediction (NSP).5 Despite its simplicity, we demonstrate in Section 5.1 that pre-training towards this task is very beneﬁcial to both QA and NLI.
items.why: Claims next sentence prediction pre-training directly benefits QA and NLI tasks.
items.plain: Despite its simplicity, we show in Section 5.1 that pre-training on next sentence prediction significantly helps question answering and natural language inference.

items.text: The “Average” column is slightly different than the ofﬁcial GLUE score, since we exclude the problematic WNLI set.8 BERT and OpenAI GPT are singlemodel, single task.

items.plain: The average column differs slightly from the official GLUE score because we excluded the problematic WNLI dataset.

items.text: Additionally, for BERTLARGE we found that ﬁnetuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets, so we ran several random restarts and selected the best model on the Dev set.
items.why: Notes fine-tuning instability on small datasets requiring multiple random restarts.
items.plain: For BERTLARGE, fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets, so we ran multiple random restarts and picked the model with the best score on the development set.

items.text: Note that BERTBASE and OpenAI GPT are nearly identical in terms of model architecture apart from the attention masking.
items.why: Asserts BERTBASE and OpenAI GPT match in architecture except attention masking.
items.plain: Note that BERTBASE and OpenAI GPT share almost identical model architectures, except for how they mask attention.

items.plain: The top entries on the SQuAD leaderboard do not have published system descriptions and are permitted to use any public training data.

items.plain: Because of this, we used modest data augmentation by fine-tuning on TriviaQA before fine-tuning on SQuAD.

items.plain: Without the TriviaQA tuning data, our model loses only 0.1 to 0.4 F1 points and still beats all existing systems by a large margin.

items.text: The left-only constraint was also applied at ﬁne-tuning, because removing it introduced a pre-train/ﬁne-tune mismatch that degraded downstream performance.
items.why: Explains left-only constraint was kept during fine-tuning to prevent mismatch.
items.plain: We kept the left-only constraint during fine-tuning because removing it created a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning that degraded downstream task performance.

items.plain: This left-to-right model is directly comparable to OpenAI GPT, but it uses our larger training dataset, input representation, and fine-tuning setup.

items.why: Claims removing next sentence prediction significantly harms performance on three tasks.
items.plain: In Table 5, we show that removing the next sentence prediction task significantly hurts performance on QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD 1.1.

items.text: The LTR model performs worse than the MLM model on all tasks, with large drops on MRPC and SQuAD.
items.why: Reports left-to-right model performs worse across all evaluated downstream tasks.
items.plain: The left-to-right model performs worse than the masked language model on all tasks, experiencing large performance drops on MRPC and SQuAD.

items.why: Notes adding a BiLSTM to LTR model degrades performance on GLUE tasks.
items.plain: Adding the BiLSTM hurts performance on the GLUE tasks.

items.text: However: (a) this is twice as expensive as a single bidirectional model; (b) this is non-intuitive for tasks like QA, since the RTL model would not be able to condition the answer on the question; (c) this it is strictly less powerful than a deep bidirectional model, since it can use both left and right context at every layer.
items.why: Argues separate LTR and RTL models are more costly and inherently weaker.
items.plain: Training separate left-to-right and right-to-left models is twice as expensive, unintuitive for question answering, and strictly less powerful than a deep bidirectional model because each layer cannot use both contexts.

items.text: We can see that larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets, even for MRPC which only has 3,600 labeled training examples, and is substantially different from the pre-training tasks.
items.why: Claims larger model size strictly improves accuracy even on tiny datasets.
items.plain: Larger models strictly improve accuracy across all four datasets, even on MRPC, which has only 3,600 labeled training examples and differs greatly from the pre-training tasks.

items.text: However, we believe that this is the ﬁrst work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided that the model has been sufﬁciently pre-trained.
items.why: Claims first proof that extreme model scaling helps very small-scale tasks.
items.plain: We believe this is the first work to convincingly show that scaling to extreme model sizes also yields large gains on very small tasks, provided the model is sufficiently pre-trained.

items.text: Both of these prior works used a featurebased approach — we hypothesize that when the model is ﬁne-tuned directly on the downstream tasks and uses only a very small number of randomly initialized additional parameters, the taskspeciﬁc models can beneﬁt from the larger, more expressive pre-trained representations even when downstream task data is very small.
items.why: Hypothesizes fine-tuning with few new parameters lets small tasks benefit from large models.
items.plain: We hypothesize that fine-tuning directly on downstream tasks with very few new randomly initialized parameters allows small datasets to benefit from larger, more expressive pre-trained representations.

items.text: First, not all tasks can be easily represented by a Transformer encoder architecture, and therefore require a task-speciﬁc model architecture to be added.
items.why: States limitation that not all tasks easily fit Transformer encoder architectures.
items.plain: First, not all tasks are easily represented by a Transformer encoder, requiring a custom model architecture to be added.

items.text: The best performing method concatenates the token representations from the top four hidden layers of the pre-trained Transformer, which is only 0.3 F1 behind ﬁne-tuning the entire model.
items.why: Shows feature-based layer concatenation performs close to full model fine-tuning.
items.plain: The best-performing feature-based method concatenates token representations from the top four hidden layers of the pre-trained Transformer, placing it only 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuning the entire model.

items.text: Compared to standard langauge model training, the masked LM only make predictions on 15% of tokens in each batch, which suggests that more pre-training steps may be required for the model
items.why: Acknowledges potential inefficiency from masking only 15% of tokens per batch.
items.plain: Because masked language modeling only predicts 15% of tokens in each batch, it may require more pre-training steps than standard language model training.

items.text: In Section C.1 we demonstrate that MLM does converge marginally slower than a leftto-right model (which predicts every token), but the empirical improvements of the MLM model far outweigh the increased training cost.
items.why: Claims empirical performance gains outweigh masked language modeling's slower pre-training convergence.
items.plain: Masked language modeling converges slightly slower than a left-to-right model that predicts every token, but its practical performance improvements far exceed the additional training cost.

items.text: The core argument of this work is that the bi-directionality and the two pretraining tasks presented in Section 3.1 account for the majority of the empirical improvements, but we do note that there are several other differences between how BERT and GPT were trained:
items.why: Identifies confounding differences between BERT and GPT baseline besides model architecture.
items.plain: Beyond model architecture, BERT and GPT differ in training data, special tokens learned during pre-training, batch sizes, and fine-tuning learning rates.

items.text: • GPT is trained on the BooksCorpus (800M words); BERT is trained on the BooksCorpus (800M words) and Wikipedia (2,500M words).
items.why: Identifies dataset scale confounder between BERT and GPT baselines.
items.plain: GPT is trained on BooksCorpus with 800 million words, whereas BERT uses BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia for a total of 3.3 billion words.

items.text: • GPT was trained for 1M steps with a batch size of 32,000 words; BERT was trained for 1M steps with a batch size of 128,000 words.
items.why: Identifies pre-training batch size confounder between BERT and GPT baselines.
items.plain: GPT was trained for 1 million steps with a batch size of 32,000 words, while BERT was trained for 1 million steps with a batch size of 128,000 words.

items.text: • GPT used the same learning rate of 5e-5 for all ﬁne-tuning experiments; BERT chooses a task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning learning rate which performs the best on the development set.
items.why: Identifies hyperparameter tuning confounder between BERT and GPT fine-tuning.
items.plain: GPT used a fixed learning rate of 5e-5 for all fine-tuning, whereas BERT searched for a task-specific learning rate that performed best on the validation set.

items.text: The GLUE webpage notes that there are issues with the construction of this dataset, 15 and every trained system that’s been submitted to GLUE has performed worse than the 65.1 baseline accuracy of predicting the majority class.
items.why: Notes dataset quality flaw where all trained systems perform below baseline.
items.plain: The Winograd NLI dataset has construction issues, causing every trained system submitted to the GLUE benchmark to perform worse than a 65.1% majority-class baseline.

items.text: Answer: Yes, BERTBASE achieves almost 1.0% additional accuracy on MNLI when trained on 1M steps compared to 500k steps.
items.why: Claims significant accuracy gains require doubling pre-training steps to 1M.
items.plain: Training the base BERT model for 1 million steps gives almost 1.0% higher accuracy on the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference dataset compared to training for 500,000 steps.

items.text: However, in terms of absolute accuracy the MLM model begins to outperform the LTR model almost immediately.
items.why: Claims masked language modeling outperforms left-to-right despite slower initial convergence.
items.plain: Although masked language modeling converges slightly slower, its absolute accuracy surpasses the left-to-right model almost immediately.

items.text: Note that the purpose of the masking strategies is to reduce the mismatch between pre-training and ﬁne-tuning, as the [MASK] symbol never appears during the ﬁne-tuning stage.
items.why: States motivation for complex masking strategy to prevent pre-train/fine-tune mismatch.
items.plain: The special masking strategies aim to reduce discrepancies between pre-training and fine-tuning, since the mask token never appears during fine-tuning.

items.text: From the table it can be seen that ﬁne-tuning is surprisingly robust to different masking strategies.
items.why: Reports ablation finding that fine-tuning is surprisingly robust to masking variations.
items.plain: Fine-tuning accuracy remains surprisingly stable across different pre-training masking strategies.

items.text: However, as expected, using only the MASK strategy was problematic when applying the featurebased approach to NER.
items.why: Identifies failure case of 100% masking when using feature-based representations.
items.plain: Using only the mask symbol during pre-training causes performance problems when applying the feature-based approach to named entity recognition.
